name: For Good
tagline: Nobody remembers the problem. That's how you know you fixed it.
epigraph: One idea behind this glass came from a convenience store.
glassware: a large stemmed goblet (about 350 ml), chilled, no salt rim
language_row: Wren's Resonance on reading v3: ready. Line that lands: "You'll happily spend a weekend on something so you never have to spend ten minutes on it again." Horoscope check: 13 of 14 sentences specific, 1 borderline held by its context. Swap test clean against *Left Standing*, *Off-Label*, *Serviceable*, *Not Only the Way*, *Not Too Polite*, *Down the Line*. Sibling echoes moved off: "that's just how it is" (*Serviceable*) → "it's always been like that"; "a renowned classic" (*Not Only the Way*); "half a teaspoon of" (*Beside the First*). His blender line is paraphrased with attribution (one-voice rule). Pronoun warnings accepted by Wren: "he", "his", "him" are Mariano Martinez, never the guest. ✓
sources: Studio fact card `_studio/fact-cards/mariano-martinez-frozen-margarita.md` (*Oxford Companion* MARGARITA pdf 1237, FROZEN DAIQUIRI pdf 854, COINTREAU pdf 551; Smithsonian NMAH object record 2005.0226.01; AP via History News Network, 10 Oct 2005; Michele Herrmann, *VinePair*, 28 March 2021, for his own words). Drink: Dave Arnold, *Liquid Intelligence* pp. 141–142 (the freezer batch, "a 7-Eleven-style frozen treat"), p. 271 (vanilla with orange); *Flavor Matrix* pdf 256 (vanilla and citrus), pdf 40 (avocado, consulted and set aside); *Cocktail Codex* p. 156; 21 CFR 169.175 (vanilla extract). Room notes: `work/explorer-creator/`.
names_note: **For Good**, the room's pick (Hester and Tomás r4; Wren conceded r5): fixed for good, and done for other people's good (his "I was just trying to make my customers happy"); beside the tagline it completes to "fixed for good". **Every Time** was Wren's r4 pick; she moved because it describes the batch, not the person, and y4 already says it. Also considered: *Not Even Cold*, *Borrowed* (Hester), *Fixed*, *Ten Minutes* (Tomás), *Once and for All*, *Properly Cold* (Wren). Rejected: *Never Again*, anything with "slush", "frozen" or "machine", *Soft Serve*, *7-Eleven*.
open_items: **No year (Hester C1):** Oxford contradicts itself (1971 in MARGARITA, 1973 in FROZEN DAIQUIRI), so the reading says no year.

**The Slurpee's own origin (C2):** the Smithsonian record says the Slurpee machine was invented in Dallas in 1960; Hester couldn't confirm it, so it stays out. The Slurpee was the idea; the machine he adapted was a soft-serve ice-cream machine (C3). His own "we developed" (C4): never a lone inventor.
**The 7-Eleven coincidence:** Arnold's "7-Eleven-style frozen treat" (*LI* p. 141) and Martinez's Slurpee at a 7-Eleven (Smithsonian, AP) are owned in one clause; Arnold never mentions Martinez.

**Strength (Tomás):** each drink holds about two standard drinks, the same size as Martinez's own printed serve; nothing in the copy calls it light. It's a batch for four in two bags; blenders do single drinks badly (*LI* p. 141).

**balance.py style:** run as freeform, because the blended style assumes ice melting into the drink and a freezer batch has none; measured against Arnold's own freezer daiquiri (14.2% / 8.4 g / 0.93%). Substitute floor: a clear orange triple sec at 40% (a 35 g/100 ml triple sec breaks his 9 g sugar cap).

**Kept out on purpose:** Oxford's sniff at frozen drinks; the grain-alcohol story; any comparison with his recipe ("never 'his recipe'"); the patent (never patented, per the museum; dossier only); Tommy's (*Half a Rim*); salt (*Making the Calls*); "slush" and "overnight". The ice-cream-counter link is the bartender's own association.
